query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated CALPHAD-plus-machine-learning approach, leveraging ab initio data and validated by high-throughput DSC measurements, can provide accurate determinations of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy composition space.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or consolidated multi-principal-element alloys without extensive prior thermodynamic characterization.
generation.intervention: Simultaneous computational design using CALPHAD-based high-throughput calculations, supplemented by ab initio thermodynamic data, integrated with iterative machine-learning updates from small-scale DSC experiments.
generation.conditions: Subject a diverse set of equiatomic and near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy compositions (covering 5–35 at.% per element) to repeated computational-experimental iterations, measuring key thermophysical parameters in the temperature range from the solidus to fully molten states.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined CALPHAD databases capturing the phases and enthalpic/entropic contributions, guided by local atomic configurations derived from ab initio data and validated by high-throughput thermal analysis.
generation.mechanism: By using physically informed feature engineering from ab initio calculations in tandem with feedback from iterative small-scale DSC measurements, the machine-learning model systematically improves the thermodynamic descriptions, providing robust predictions of melting-related properties across vast HEA composition spaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate (within ~5–10% of measured values) property predictions, including melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting over a wide variety of high-entropy alloys.
generation.baseline: Existing purely experimental or purely first-principles approaches provide either incomplete coverage of the large composition space or impose high computational/experimental costs.
generation.boundary: Requires an adequate baseline of thermodynamic data for calibration and may lose reliability for compositions beyond the established domains of the CALPHAD and machine-learning models.
generation.uncertainty: Limited training data and potential inaccuracies in reference thermodynamic databases could lead to systematic errors if not periodically corrected by targeted experimental reference measurements.

falsification_experiment.design: Select multiple HEA compositions spanning a broad range of principal elements. Cast small ingots, then measure melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volumetric changes via DSC and in-situ diffraction. Compare the measurements with property predictions from the integrated model, across the entire composition set, to identify systematic errors.
measurements: Volume change upon melting (dilatometry or in-situ diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If measured thermophysical properties deviate consistently from predicted values by more than ~10% across the sampled compositions, or fail to match composition trends, the proposed integrated CALPHAD–machine-learning framework is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: A 2021 study employed high-throughput computational screening to survey thousands of prospective high-entropy alloy compositions, successfully pinpointing those with high melting points in an Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system. This method accelerated discovery by focusing on stability and phase prediction but did not directly provide key thermophysical properties such as enthalpy/entropy of fusion or volume change at melting. Despite demonstrating the feasibility of computational scanning for melting behaviors, comprehensive coverage of liquid-phase thermodynamics and verification across the broader range of multi-principal-element alloys remain incomplete, highlighting the need for more robust data collection and validation strategies.
decision.unsolved: A scalable method to accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamics across the entire HEA composition space is still lacking. While computational predictions can guide alloy selection, substantial challenges persist in calibrating and validating these predictions experimentally for complex, compositionally diverse systems.
decision.lever: An integrated CALPHAD and machine-learning framework incorporating ab initio thermodynamic data with small-scale, high-throughput thermal analysis (e.g., differential scanning calorimetry). Key parameters include systematic coverage of multi-element composition space, physically informed feature engineering, and iterative machine-learning updates based on validation experiments.
decision.why: This approach builds on the high-throughput computational screening trend and extends it to bridge the gap in experimental thermophysical data near melting. By coupling predictive modeling with targeted small-sample measurements, the methodology can rapidly converge on accurate predictions of Tm, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volumetric changes at melting. A decisive validation would compare predicted vs. measured thermodynamic profiles across a suitably large set of compositions; consistent, quantitative agreement would confirm viability, while systematic deviations beyond experimental and model uncertainty would invalidate the approach.
